title: WHY SAUL ALMOST KILLED HIS OWN SON OVER A SPOONFUL OF HONEY
paragraphs:
WHY SAUL ALMOST KILLED HIS OWN SON OVER A SPOONFUL OF HONEY
Jonathan tasted a little honey. His eyes brightened. Minutes later, his father was prepared to execute him—and buried inside this disturbing story is a warning about what happens when religious zeal becomes more important than the heart of God.
Imagine winning a battle for your nation...
then discovering that your own father wants you dead.
Not because you betrayed him.
Not because you joined the enemy.
Not because you murdered someone.
Not because you abandoned God.
Because you tasted honey.
A little honey.
That is how strange—and terrifying—the scene in 1 Samuel 14 becomes.
Jonathan stands before King Saul, who is not merely his king.
He is his father.
The soldiers are watching.
The battlefield is still stained with the exhaustion of war.
And Saul asks his son what he has done.
Jonathan answers with devastating simplicity.
“טָעֹם טָעַמְתִּי בִּקְצֵה הַמַּטֶּה אֲשֶׁר־בְּיָדִי מְעַט דְּבַשׁ”
Ta‘om ta‘amti... me‘at devash.
“I tasted a little honey...”
The Hebrew word דְּבַשׁ (devash) means honey.
And me‘at means little, a small amount.
Jonathan is essentially saying:
I only tasted a little honey.
Then comes the sentence no son should ever hear from his father:
“You shall surely die, Jonathan.”
How did they get here?
How does a father become so committed to something he has said that he is prepared to kill his own son rather than admit that perhaps his own judgment was disastrously wrong?
And before we condemn Saul from a comfortable distance, there is another question waiting for us.
How often do we do smaller versions of the same thing?
How often does pride disguise itself as conviction?
How often does control disguise itself as spiritual leadership?
How often do we defend something simply because we said it?
How often do we invoke God while quietly protecting ourselves?
Because the most frightening thing about Saul in this story is not merely that he made a foolish oath.
It is that he became willing to sacrifice someone else to preserve it.
And the story begins before Jonathan ever tastes the honey.
Israel is fighting the Philistines.

Jonathan has already demonstrated extraordinary faith. Earlier in the chapter, he and his armor-bearer approach a Philistine outpost with words that reveal something Saul increasingly struggles to understand:
“Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.”
Jonathan does not presume upon God.
He trusts God's power.
And God gives an astonishing victory.
Confusion erupts through the Philistine camp. Israel advances.
This should have been a day remembered for God's deliverance.
But Saul introduces something God had not commanded.
He places the army under an oath.
No one is to eat until evening, until Saul has taken vengeance upon his enemies.
Notice the language.
Not simply God's enemies.
“My enemies.”
That detail should bother us.
Saul's leadership is becoming increasingly entangled with Saul's ego.
And because of his command, exhausted soldiers march into a forest where honey is literally available to them...
and nobody touches it.
Picture that.
Men depleted from battle.
Bodies desperate for energy.
Food sitting in front of them.
Honey dripping.
Yet they are terrified to eat.
Scripture says they feared the oath.
Then Jonathan enters the forest.
But Jonathan has one enormous disadvantage.
He never heard what Saul said.
That matters.
A lot.
The biblical text explicitly tells us that Jonathan “had not heard” his father place the people under the oath.
So Jonathan is not sneaking through the woods thinking, I know what my father commanded, but I don't care.
That would fundamentally change the story.
He does not knowingly violate Saul's command.
He simply sees honey.
He stretches out the staff in his hand.
Touches its tip to the honeycomb.
Brings the honey to his mouth.
And eats.
Then Scripture gives us one of those beautiful little details that makes the scene almost visible:
His eyes brighten.
The Hebrew expression is vivid:
וַתָּאֹרְנָה עֵינָיו
Vatta'ornah ‘einav.
His eyes became bright.
Life returns to him.
His strength revives.
Then someone tells him what happened.
Your father made everyone swear an oath.
Anyone who eats today is cursed.
Jonathan's response is revealing.
He does not suddenly panic because he believes he has rebelled against God.
Instead, he recognizes what Saul's command has done to the nation.
“My father has troubled the land.”
Jonathan sees what prideful leadership often cannot see:
A command can sound spiritual while producing terrible fruit.
Saul's oath weakened the very people who were fighting.
The soldiers became desperately hungry. Later they rushed upon the spoil and ate meat improperly with the blood, violating an actual divine prohibition.
That contrast is uncomfortable.
Saul's man-made restriction did not make the people holier.
It helped create conditions in which exhausted people fell into actual sin.
There is a warning here for every parent.
Every pastor.
Every ministry leader.
Every husband.
Every wife.
Every teacher.
Every Christian with influence over another human being.
We must never confuse our personal rules with God's commandments.
There is a difference between saying:
“God has spoken.”
and saying:
“This is what I prefer.”
There is a difference between biblical conviction and personal control.
There is a difference between obedience to Scripture and loyalty to somebody's ego.
And whenever those lines become blurred, people get hurt.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe nobody threatened to execute you over honey.
But perhaps you grew up believing God was perpetually angry because someone represented Him that way.
Maybe every mistake became a catastrophe.
Maybe every question was treated as rebellion.
Maybe you learned how to look spiritual while becoming terrified inside.
Maybe you were taught dozens of rules...
but very little grace.
Maybe someone made you feel that disappointing them meant disappointing God.
And perhaps, years later, you still struggle to distinguish the voice of your heavenly Father from the voice of human fear.
Hear this carefully:
Biblical Christianity is not freedom from obedience.
Jesus calls us to obedience.
Jesus calls us to repentance.
Jesus calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
Grace is not permission to redefine sin.
But neither are human beings permitted to redefine their preferences as the commandments of God.
Scripture must remain Scripture.
God's commands remain God's commands.
Our opinions remain our opinions.
That distinction can save people from enormous spiritual damage.
And Saul was losing it.
Eventually Saul seeks an answer concerning why God has not responded.
The lot falls upon Jonathan.
Saul demands:
“Tell me what you have done.”
Jonathan confesses exactly what happened.
He tasted a little honey with the end of his staff.
Nothing hidden.
Nothing embellished.
Nothing defended.
Then Jonathan accepts the consequences Saul intends to impose.
And Saul responds:
“You shall surely die, Jonathan.”
Think about that moment.
This is the son who had just fought courageously.
The son through whom God had worked.
The son whose faith helped trigger Israel's deliverance.
Saul is prepared to lose him.
Why?
Because Saul has trapped himself inside his own words.
This is what pride eventually does.
It makes admitting you were wrong feel more painful than hurting someone you love.
Read that again.
Pride makes admitting you were wrong feel more painful than hurting someone you love.
That destroys marriages.
It destroys friendships.
It destroys churches.
It destroys families.
Someone knows they spoke too harshly...
but apologizing feels humiliating.
Someone realizes their accusation was wrong...
but they keep defending it.
A father knows he wounded his child...
but says, “I'm still your father.”
A ministry leader realizes a decision harmed people...
but fears losing authority if he admits it.
A Christian discovers that something he passionately taught cannot actually be defended from Scripture...
but protecting his reputation becomes more important than correcting the error.
And eventually the issue is no longer truth.
It is ego.
That is the cliff Saul is standing on.
But then something extraordinary happens.
The people refuse.
The king says Jonathan must die.
The people say no.
“Shall Jonathan die, who has accomplished this great salvation in Israel?”
Absolutely not.
They recognize something Saul's obsession has blinded him to.
God had been working through Jonathan.
Then Scripture says:
“So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.”
The Hebrew verb behind “rescued/ransomed” in the verse is פדה (padah), a word associated with ransoming or redeeming.
Jonathan is spared.
Saul's sentence does not have the final word.

And although we must be careful not to pretend every Old Testament event is a direct one-to-one prophecy of Jesus, Christians cannot read the Bible's great language of redemption without eventually arriving at the One in whom redemption reaches its fulfillment.
Because Jonathan was rescued from a sentence of death.
But the Gospel tells an even greater story.
We were not merely victims of somebody else's foolish oath.
We actually sinned.
We actually rebelled.
We actually stand guilty before a holy God.
Our deepest problem is not merely that people have wounded us.
Our deepest problem is that sin has separated humanity from God.
And Jesus did not come merely to make exhausted people feel better about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
The astonishing scandal of Christianity is that the truly innocent Son was not spared.
Jesus Christ, unlike Jonathan, was perfectly innocent.
No deceit.
No hidden rebellion.
No secret corruption.
No sin.
Yet at the cross, Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The Apostle Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
The righteous...
for the unrighteous.
That is the Gospel.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Not God lowering His holiness.
Not humanity rescuing itself.
Jesus bearing sin and conquering death so that those who repent and trust in Him may be forgiven, reconciled, redeemed, and made new.
Jonathan tasted honey and faced a sentence he had not knowingly provoked.
Jesus tasted suffering He did not deserve so guilty people could receive mercy they could never earn.
And maybe that is where this ancient battlefield suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are still trying to live like Saul.
We would rather preserve our image than surrender our pride.
We would rather appear right than repent.
We would rather make excuses than confess.
We would rather control people than trust God.
We would rather announce religious promises than quietly obey what God has already said.
And Jesus is calling us out of that prison.
Maybe the person who needs grace today is your son.
Your daughter.
Your spouse.
Your parent.
Your friend.
Maybe you have been demanding payment for something Christ is asking you to release.
Maybe you have weaponized silence.
Maybe you keep replaying somebody's failure because anger makes you feel powerful.
Maybe your household has learned to fear your mood more than they trust your love.
Maybe the apology should have happened years ago.
Or maybe you are Jonathan in this story.
You have lived beneath someone else's impossible expectations.
You were punished for rules you never understood.
You were blamed for wounds you did not create.
You have carried words spoken over you as though they were God's final verdict.
“Failure.”
“Useless.”
“Unlovable.”
“Too damaged.”
“Too dirty.”
“Too far gone.”
But human words are not the throne of God.
And your worst chapter does not outrank the cross.
The Gospel does not tell you that everything you have done is acceptable.
It tells you something infinitely better:
There is forgiveness for sinners in Jesus Christ.
Real forgiveness.
Purchased at a real cross.
Confirmed by an empty tomb.
Offered to people who could never clean themselves enough to deserve it.
This is why repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is coming home to truth.
It is dropping the excuses.
Dropping the performance.
Dropping the religious mask.
Dropping the exhausting attempt to save yourself.
And saying:
Jesus, I need mercy.
Maybe your “honey” is something hidden.
Something seemingly small.
A compromise.
A resentment.
A secret habit.
A lie you keep feeding.
A pride you keep protecting.
Do not twist Jonathan's story into saying his innocent taste of honey was secretly sinful—the text tells us he did not know about Saul's oath.
But allow his story to ask you a different question:
What happens when what we want becomes more authoritative to us than what God has actually said?
That was Saul's danger.
And it can become ours.
Because religious language cannot sanctify pride.
Quoting God does not automatically mean God endorses our motives.
Having authority does not make every decision righteous.
Making a vow does not transform foolishness into wisdom.
And being embarrassed about admitting we were wrong does not give us permission to continue hurting people.
Sometimes the most spiritual sentence you can say is:
“I was wrong.”
Sometimes revival begins with:
“Forgive me.”
Sometimes a marriage begins healing when somebody stops winning arguments.
Sometimes a father becomes stronger the moment his children finally hear him apologize.
Sometimes a believer becomes free when they stop defending what Jesus is asking them to surrender.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Transforming grace.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and still opens the door to restoration.
Grace that confronts us without abandoning us.
Grace that does not leave us where it found us.
Grace that takes scandals and writes redemption across them.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
From scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
What am I defending because admitting I was wrong would cost my pride?
Sit with that.
Do not answer quickly.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has already brought a name to mind.
A conversation.
A wound.
A secret.
A person you need to forgive.
A person from whom you need to ask forgiveness.
A sin you need to confess.

And if Christ has already been rebuilding something in you that you thought was permanently destroyed, tell us. Your testimony might become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needs tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
But if this truth glorifies Christ, carrying it to another person can be a simple act of witness.
Someone may be becoming Saul without realizing it.
Someone may be Jonathan—wounded, confused, wondering whether God is as cruel as the people who misrepresented Him.
Come back when pride starts whispering that apologizing is weakness.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Sometimes one faithful piece of Scripture placed in front of someone at the right moment becomes the beginning of a much larger conversation about eternity.
It cannot.
Not because supporting a ministry earns salvation.
It never will.
Jesus alone saves.
Your support helps us keep putting Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, discipleship resources, and messages of repentance and grace in front of people who need them.
If you have been reading quietly for months, perhaps this is the moment to help carry the message farther.
Again, sharing does not make you more righteous before God.
But if you believe Jesus Christ should be proclaimed, do not underestimate what God can do when ordinary believers stop treating the Gospel as something meant to remain private.
One share.
One tag.
One conversation.
One person reading at two in the morning while nobody else knows they are falling apart.
One exhausted believer discovering that human religious cruelty is not the same thing as the heart of Christ.
One proud father deciding to apologize.
One wounded son deciding to forgive.
One sinner finally whispering:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That is why we keep writing.
Because behind every screen is a soul.
Behind every profile is a story.
Behind every polished photograph may be a battle nobody sees.
And above every human story stands a Savior whose grace is greater than our worst chapter.
Saul almost allowed a little honey to cost him his son.
Do not let pride cost you yours.
Do not let pride cost you your marriage.
Do not let pride cost you your church.
Do not let pride cost you years you can never recover.
And above all, do not cling to pride while Jesus is offering mercy.
Come into the light.
Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive as one who has been forgiven.
Make the phone call.
Have the conversation.
Confess the truth.
Open the Bible again.
Come back to Christ.
Because the sweetest thing in 1 Samuel 14 was never really the honey.
It was mercy having the final word over a sentence of death.
And thousands of years later, at a cross outside Jerusalem, mercy would speak louder still.
When pride says, “Someone must pay,” look again at the cross—Jesus already did.
